b.bio: Luc d'Achery (Latinized Lucas Acherius), born at Saint-Quentin in Picardy, entered the Benedictines young and was professed at Trinity Abbey, Vendôme, on 4 October 1632; poor health soon moved him to Paris, where he joined St-Germain-des-Prés in 1637 and stayed nearly fifty years until his death there on 29 April 1685. As librarian he became a leading bibliographical authority on unedited medieval writings, corresponding with monasteries across and beyond France. He edited the Epistle of Barnabas (1645), the complete works of Lanfranc (1648), and first published Guibert of Nogent's works (1661). The items under this name in this library are his editorial apparatus — admonitions, notices, dedicatory letters, prolegomena, and notes — prefixed to texts across the Patrologia Latina.
b.s: The works here are not independent treatises but d'Achery's editorial prefaces and annotations to medieval authors he printed, including his edition of Guibert of Nogent; a reader holding them holds the scholarship that made these texts available.

b.bio: Ludwig Konrad Bethmann, born in Helmstedt and died in Wolfenbüttel, was a German historian, philologist, and librarian. He studied at Göttingen under Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm, Karl Otfried Müller, and Friedrich Christoph Dahlmann, took his doctorate at Jena in 1838, and worked intermittently from 1834 (continuously from 1837) until 1854 under Georg Heinrich Pertz on the Monumenta Germaniae Historica, editing some thirty texts including Sigebert of Gembloux's world chronicle (1844). Manuscript journeys took him through Holland, Belgium, France, Italy, Greece, and Egypt. From 1854 until his death he directed the Ducal Library at Wolfenbüttel.
b.s: The pieces held here are not patristic texts but Bethmann's editorial apparatus: prolegomena, notices, and his edition of the Bertinian genealogies of the Counts of Flanders, in which he argues that the Bertinian recension is the source of all later versions and is witnessed by six manuscripts.

Wilhelm Wattenbach (1819–1897) — Wilhelm Wattenbach (born Rantzau, Holstein, 22 September 1819; died Frankfurt, 20 September 1897) was a German historian. He studied philology at Bonn, Göttingen and Berlin, joined the Monumenta Germaniae Historica in 1843, became archivist at Breslau in 1855, professor at Heidelberg in 1862 and at Berlin in 1873, where he sat on the MGH central directorate from 1875 and chaired it 1886–88. His principal work was Deutschlands Geschichtsquellen im Mittelalter bis zur Mitte des XIII Jahrhunderts (1858), a guide to medieval German sources; he also wrote manuals of Greek and Latin palaeography and Das Schriftwesen im Mittelalter.
b.s: The pieces held here are not patristic texts but Bethmann's editorial apparatus: prolegomena, notices, and his edition of the Bertinian genealogies of the Counts of Flanders, in which he argues that the Bertinian recension is the source of all later versions and is witnessed by six manuscripts.

b.bio: Louis-Georges-Oudard-Feudrix de Bréquigny, born in Normandy in 1714, was a French historian and scholar, not a church father. From 1754 he was charged with completing the Ordonnances des Rois de France de la 3e Race, publishing five further volumes up to 1790. He wrote for the Académie des Inscriptions an Histoire de Posthume empereur des Gaules and a Mémoire sur l'établissement de la religion et de l'empire de Mahomet, was elected to the Académie française in 1772, and after the Seven Years' War was sent to search English archives for documents on French history, bringing back thousands of document copies now held at the Bibliothèque nationale. Sources disagree on his death date: 3 July 1795 (Wikipedia, Académie française, 1911 Britannica) versus 2 July 1794 in Paris (Britannica). His appearance under 'Latin Fathers' is as an editor: the two short Prolegomena held here are his prefatory matter to a volume of Migne's Patrologia Latina.
b.s: The works here are editorial prefaces he supplied for Migne's Patrologia Latina, vol. 87, not patristic writings of his own.

b.bio:
Brequigny, Louis-Georges-Oudard de (unknown) — The library holds one page under this name in Migne's Patrologia Latina (PL 214), an 'Admonition'. No source identifies its author. The biographical sources found describe Louis-Georges-Oudard-Feudrix de Bréquigny (1714–1795), an eighteenth-century French historian and editor of the Ordonnances des Rois de France — a different person, of a different century and tradition, whose works do not match the patristic item shelved here. That identification is therefore set aside, and nothing can be asserted about the author of the Admonition beyond what PL 214 itself contains.

La Porte du Theil, Franc (unknown) — the surviving records describe François-Jean-Gabriel de La Porte du Theil (1742–1815), a French historian and hellenist of the Académie des Inscriptions et Belles-Lettres who worked on the Rosetta Stone Greek text and translated Aeschylus and Callimachus. That man belongs to the eighteenth century and wrote no patristic admonition. He is not established to be the author of the single-page Admonition printed under this name in PL 214, which the library holds; the two must be kept apart.
b.s: The single work held here is a one-page 'Admonition' printed in PL 214; its authorship remains unestablished.

b.bio: Cellot was born in Paris in 1588 and entered the Society of Jesus at Nancy in 1605. He taught humanities and rhetoric for sixteen years and held a chair of Scripture for seven, served as rector of the colleges at Rouen and La Flèche, and became provincial of the French province from 1654. His order charged him with defending the privileges of the regulars against the rights of parish pastors, the controversy behind his De Hierarchia et Hierarchis (Rouen, 1641), which the Sorbonne censured and Rome placed on the Index. He also wrote against Hallier (Horarum subcesivarum, Paris, 1648), a history of Gottschalk (1655), and an account of the Council of Douzy (1658), besides poetry and drama. He died in Paris on 20 October 1658.
b.s: The library holds only a six-page historical notice from him in PL 124, the Patrologia Latina volume devoted to Gottschalk, presumably connected to his Historia Gotteschalci of 1655.

b.bio: The library's record points to the Second Lateran Council, held at Rome in 1139. The two-page decree printed here matches its canons: it condemns the antipope Burdinus (Gregory, who had taken the name Gregory VIII) and his followers, the porticani, and legislates against simoniacal and irregular ordination. Source 3 confirms only that a Lateran council was held in 1139; the identification of the decree with that assembly rests on the library record itself.
b.s: Its canons on void ordinations by heretics, canonical election of bishops, clerical celibacy, and lay seizure of church property were incorporated into Gratian's Decretum and so entered the mainstream of canon law; readers here hold the conciliar text itself, aimed at Burdinus and the porticani.

b.bio: Louis Ellies du Pin, born in Paris in 1657 of a noble Norman family, studied at the college of Harcourt and the Sorbonne, taking his bachelor's degree in theology in 1680 and doctorate in 1684. A disciple of the Gallican critic Jean Launoy, he published from 1686 his Nouvelle bibliothèque des auteurs ecclésiastiques, a history of Christian literature combining biography, literary criticism and doctrinal history in French rather than Latin. The work drew opposition from Bossuet, was censured by the archbishop of Paris in 1691, and was suppressed in 1696 despite Dupin's retraction.
b.s: The Preface held here introduces one volume of Migne's Patrologia Latina; Dupin matters as the pioneer of critical ecclesiastical literary history whose method shaped later patristic scholarship.

w: Prefaces to the Annals of Lambert

b.bio:
Hesse, Ludwig Friedrich (1783–1867) — Ludwig Friedrich Hesse was born in Rudolstadt on 2 September 1783, son of the conrector Johann Ludwig Hesse. He studied theology, philology and antiquities at Leipzig from 1801 and took his doctorate in 1805. He taught at the Rudolstadt Gymnasium — collaborator, subconrector (1807), professor (1810), director (1819) — while working on Thuringian and Schwarzburg history from the princely archive. From 1837 he served as archivist and librarian in Rudolstadt, later holding the title of court councillor and privy archivist. He died there on 28 March 1867. His publications include a history of the monastery Paulinzella (1815) and works on Arnstadt and Schwarzburg. The library's shelf label 'Latin Fathers' is misleading: this is a nineteenth-century German editor of medieval sources, not a patristic author.

Waitz, Georg (1813–1886) — Georg Waitz, born at Flensburg and educated at Kiel and Berlin, was a medieval historian trained under Leopold von Ranke. He joined Georg Heinrich Pertz at the Monumenta Germaniae Historica in 1836, held chairs of history at Kiel (1842–1848) and Göttingen (1849–1875), sat in the Frankfurt National Assembly in 1848, and from 1875 led the MGH as head of its Scriptores section. He is not a church father or medieval author; the library holds him here because Migne printed his critical prefaces to Lambert of Hersfeld's Annals in PL 146.
b.s: The work held here is his edition of Lambert of Hersfeld's Annals (Berlin, Besser, 1855); its prefaces argue that Lambert lived publicly before entering monastic life, that Hersfeld stood foremost among German monastic schools, that Lambert copied the lost Hersfeld annals verbatim, and that archival letters correct his errors.

w: Letters on the spits of Diana of Ephesus

b.bio: Lucas Holstenius (born Lucas Holstein at Hamburg in 1596; died at Rome, 2 February 1661) studied at Leiden among scholars such as Heinsius and Meursius, traveled in Italy and Sicily with Philip Cluverius in 1618, and gathered materials for his Geographi Minores in England from 1622. Converted to Catholicism in Paris around 1624 after reading the Greek and Latin Fathers on mystical theology, he entered Cardinal Francesco Barberini's household in Rome in 1627 as his librarian from 1636, and was later placed over the Vatican Library by Innocent X. He worked as a philologist, geographer, historian, and antiquarian, opposing strict censorship by the Congregation of the Index.
b.s: The single work held here is a set of letters on the many-breasted image of Diana of Ephesus, arguing that her statue was propped up by iron supports — defending the genuine reading 'verubus' in Minucius Felix's Octavius, where 'veru' means an oblong rod of raw iron rather than a javelin — against Fulvius Ursinus, Joseph Scaliger, Justus Lipsius, John Wower, Geverhart Elmenhorst, Peter Faber, and Jean Tristan.

w: Acts of the Assembly of Ravenna

b.bio: Surviving records do not clearly identify this author; they treat Lambert of Saint-Omer (Benedictine abbot of St-Bertin, d. 22 June 1125) and Lambert of Ardres (parish priest and chronicler, active 1194–1203), neither of whom wrote on the Synod of Formosus, tithe laws, or appeals to emperors Louis, Charles, Lothair, and Guy. The work held under this name belongs to a different, earlier Frankish writer, apparently active in the late ninth century when those rulers reigned. Nothing in the sources establishes his dates, office, or life.
b.s: The library holds his Acts of the Assembly of Ravenna (PL 138), a short historical-polemical text defending the canonicity of the Formosus synod, excommunication for non-payment of tithes, and imperial privileges of the Roman church.

b.bio: Lambert of Pult (Lambertus Pultariensis) is known only from a single letter addressed to Alberic, an abbot whose community had asked him for instruction. Writing as an old man who protests his own feebleness — he compares the request to sending a sheep to borrow wool from a goat — he supplies notes on Latin usage drawn from what he learned from his teachers and retained by long practice. The letter is grammatical, not doctrinal: it treats accentuation (usque modo with the antepenult accented), compounds in -modo, the spelling di rather than dis before most consonants, and the latinizing of Greek ei as long i, citing Priscian, Isidore, Horace, and Juvenal. He is not Lambert of Saint-Omer (12th-century encyclopedist) nor Lambert of Hersfeld (11th-century chronicler), both of whom fall outside his attested floruit.
b.s: His one surviving work is a ninth-century letter on correct Latin, showing how Carolingian monks taught usage, reason, and authority as the tests of correctness.

b.bio: Lambert of Squillace is known to the sources only through the Statuta printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina under his name, dated 1125. The name points to Squillace, the Latin diocese in Calabria whose history runs from late antiquity through Byzantine occupation and Norman-era reform. Nothing else about his life or office is attested here; he should not be confused with other medieval Lamberts.
b.s: His single surviving work records early twelfth-century fasting discipline: seasonal fasts attributed to a Master Bruno, dispensation for the infirm, monastic fasting after Benedict's rule, and abstinence from lacticinia beginning at Septuagesima.

b.bio: Landry (Landericus) was chief clerk of the royal chancery before succeeding Audobertus as Bishop of Paris around 650, under Clovis II. During the famine of 650–51 he sold his possessions and church vessels to feed the poor, and is credited with founding a hospital dedicated to St. Christopher that became the Hôtel-Dieu. In 653 he subscribed, with twenty-three other bishops, to Clovis II's charter exempting Saint-Denis Abbey from episcopal jurisdiction — the document held here in PL 87. One source gives his death as 656; most give about 661.
b.s: The work held here is the subscription to the Saint-Denis privilege charter issued by Clovis II, an early witness to monastic exemption claims: immunity from episcopal dues and synods, abbatial jurisdiction over injuries to exempt clerics, and free chrism and oil for exempt clergy.

b.bio: Landolfus Sagax was a Langobard historian writing in the Beneventan Duchy in the last quarter of the tenth century or the beginning of the eleventh. His Historia Romana, an expansion and continuation of Paul the Deacon's eighth-century work of the same name, was published by Pierre Pithou in Basel in 1569 under the title Historia Miscella because of its varied sources and content. It lists Byzantine emperors down to Basil II and Constantine VIII and empresses from Fausta onward, and contains exhortations to a princeps that suggest composition at a court—Naples or Benevento, which scholars dispute. A Heidelberg manuscript written in Beneventan script shows signs of Landulf's own supervision.
b.s: The library holds his Additamentum to Paul the Deacon's Historia Miscella: historical material treating rulership, almsgiving, mercy toward the repentant, and the duties of princes, with polemic against figures such as Sophia Augusta, Smaragdus the patrician, Philippicus, and Leo Augustus.

w: Histories of the City of Milan

b.bio: Landulf of Saint Paul, called Landulf Junior to distinguish him from Landulf Senior, was a Milanese historian whose life is known almost entirely from his own Historia Mediolanensis. He states he was sixty years old in 1136, giving a birth year around 1077. A nephew and student of the Pataria leader Liprando, he became an acolyte towards the end of the eleventh century — then the highest-ranking minor order in Milan — and held that rank for the rest of his life; after losing the priesthood of San Paolo around 1113, his chief ambition was to regain it, corresponding with popes and emperors to that end. He studied at Orléans during three sojourns in France when his faction was out of favour in Milan, and claims a large role in the election of Conrad of Hohenstaufen as King of Italy in 1128.
b.s: His Liber Historiarum Mediolanensis Urbis is the chief narrative source for Milan's conflict-ridden years 1097–1137, written from a partisan Pataria standpoint against Archbishop Jordan and Grossulanus.

w: History of the Translation and Miracles

b.bio: Lantfred, a monk originally from Fleury-sur-Loire who lived at Winchester in the later tenth century, was a priest and disciple of Bishop Æthelwold. He wrote an account of St Swithun's life and miracles — the Vita S. Swithuni and the Translatio et miracula S. Swithuni — together with a Vita S. Birini. He says he knew little of Swithun's life and wrote chiefly of his miracles; his Latin is inflated and obscure, with frequent Greek-derived vocabulary.
b.s: The work held here, the History of the Translation and Miracles of St Swithun (PL 155), corresponds to his Translatio et miracula S. Swithuni, the earliest account of Swithun's cult. It argues that God works miracles through the merits of the saints, against incredulous and envious deniers who deny or twist them.

b.bio: No surviving record identifies an author named 'Lawrence of Monte Cassino'. The materials consulted describe Bertharius (abbot of Monte Cassino, d. 883), Peter the Deacon and Paul the Deacon (both Cassinese monks), and Lawrence of Durham (a twelfth-century prior of Durham, a different person entirely); none concerns an author under this name. The library's single item under this name is a two-page sermon in PL 133 on the saints: their example, humility, intercession, and miracles. Its attribution to any Cassinese writer cannot be established from the sources at hand.
b.s: The work held here is a brief sermon arguing that saints teach by example more than words, that humility guards all other virtues, that true worship values inner devotion over vocal sweetness, and that saints intercede daily for the faithful.

b.bio: Lawrence of Verona is not to be confused with the better-documented figures who share his name: Lawrence of Aquilegia, a thirteenth-century Italian canon and teacher of letter-writing (ars dictaminis), or Lawrence of Brindisi (1559–1619), the Capuchin doctor of the church who joined his order at Verona in 1575. Neither source describes this author. The library holds one work under his name, On the Balearic War, printed in PL 163 (28 pages), which addresses the Christian expedition against the Moors of Balea and rebukes the murmuring Lucensian crowds and departing soldiers.
b.s: His single held work is a moralizing account of the Balearic crusade, arguing that participation in holy war must be voluntary rather than coerced, that deserters must repent their sinful wish to leave, and that God grants strength to those fighting for him.

w: Deeds of the Bishops and Abbots of Verdun

b.bio: Laurentius de Leodio (Laurent of Liège), also named Laurentius of Saint Laurent, is recorded by Deutsche Biographie with the date 1144 and by Documenta Catholica Omnia under a working range of 1150–1250; the two sources disagree on dating, and neither gives a birthplace or office beyond his association with Saint Laurent at Liège. He wrote the Gesta Virdunensium Episcoporum et Abbatum, a history of the bishops and abbots of Verdun, preserved in PL 204.
b.s: His Gesta records Verdun's episcopal succession and defends its church's rights against named opponents such as Richard of Verdun, Henry of Grand-Pré, and Emperors Henry II and IV, arguing that deeds of the fathers must be written down for imitation before mortality erases all memory.

b.bio: André Joseph Ghislain Le Glay (1785–1863), a French historian and editor of the early nineteenth century, is recorded as scientific editor with Alexandre Teulet (and with J. Guadet and N. R. Taranne as illustrators) of the Société de l'histoire de France edition of Gregory of Tours' Historiae ecclesiasticae Francorum (Paris: Renouard, 1836–1838). The works held under this name in the library are not treatises of his own but the apparatus of an editor: short historical notices prefixed to several Migne Patrologia Latina volumes (PL 105, 134, 142, 146, 160) and annotations, one of which argues against Ducange and cites Colvener, Peignot, Wibold, Baldric, and Houillon.
b.s: He matters to readers here not as a theologian but as the scholarly hand behind the historical notices and annotations accompanying several Patrologia Latina volumes; his notices on virtues and law (including an epilogue distich inviting clerics to a game of virtues, evidently touching Wibold) serve as editorial orientation to those texts.

w: Donation of the Church of Atina
Sermon on the octave of St. Mark
Sermon on the Passion of Mark
Translation of the Body of Pope Mark

b.bio: The library's record identifies this author as Leo, bishop of Atina, and the works held under his name are local hagiographical and liturgical pieces concerning St. Mark of Atina: an account of the translation of Pope Mark's body, a record of a church donation at Atina, and two sermons on Mark's passion and feast octave. None of The surviving records describes this figure; they concern other men whose names resemble his — Leo of Ostia (Marsicanus), the Monte Cassino chronicler; Terrisio di Atina, a thirteenth-century rhetorician; Peter the Deacon, who retired to Atina; and Leo of Naples, the translator of the Alexander Romance. These sources therefore cannot be used to establish facts about him, though nothing in them contradicts his identification.
b.s: His works here preserve the cult of St. Mark of Atina — his martyrdom under Domitian, the power of his relics, and visions directing that cult — as argued in the library's holdings.

b.bio:
Leo of Bourges (fl. 453) — Leo was bishop of Bourges in the mid-fifth century; the Catholic Encyclopedia records that he occupied that see in 453 and was its twelfth bishop. The work held here is an epistle printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina (PL 53), and modern scholarship treats it as a document concerning clerical immunity and the relations between clergy and secular authority in the early medieval West. Beyond his episcopal office and the date 453, the sources give no further biographical details.

Victor of Le Mans (d. by 397) — Victor was an early bishop of Le Mans whom later tradition made the father and predecessor of Victorius (or Victurius), bishop there c. 422–490. The Cult of Saints database records his reported death as not after 397, and links both bishops with Martin of Tours through the Acts of Victor and Victorius, a Latin text written probably at Le Mans or Tours around c. 700. The encyclopedia accounts of 'Victurius' describe the later homonym, not this man; they are kept separate here.

Eustochius of Tours (d. 461) — Eustochius, fifth bishop of Tours, came from an illustrious family of Auvergne; Gregory of Tours calls him a man of eminent virtue. He succeeded Brice in 444 and died in 461. At the Council of Angers (453) he defended the church's privileges against a law of Valentinian III and had a principal share in drawing up its disciplinary regulations. He increased parishes in his diocese and built a church at Tours housing relics of Gervasius and Protasius. The library holds one epistle under his name.
b.s: His surviving epistle is evidence for how a fifth-century Gallic bishop asserted the privileges of the church against secular power.

b.bio: Leo II was a Sicilian, son of a man named Paul, who became Bishop of Rome after a long delay between his election (shortly after Agatho's death on 10 January 681) and his consecration on 17 August 682 — a delay probably tied to continued correspondence with Emperor Constantine IV over imperial confirmation of papal elections. The Liber Pontificalis describes him as eloquent, versed in Scripture and both Greek and Latin, and distinguished in chanting and psalmody. His short pontificate is chiefly remembered for ratifying the acts of the Sixth Ecumenical Council (Constantinople III, 680–681) against the Monothelites, while judging that Pope Honorius I's fault lay in permissiveness toward the heresy rather than formal heresy itself.
b.s: The letters held here concern his confirmation of Constantinople III: the two natural wills and operations of Christ, the deposition of obstinate heretical bishops (including Macarius of Antioch), and the authority of Agatho's orthodox confession transmitted through Peter.

b.bio: Leo IV was a Roman, educated at the monastery of St. Martin near St. Peter's, made subdeacon by Gregory IV and cardinal-priest of Santi Quattro Coronati by Sergius II. He was elected pope in April 847 without waiting for imperial consent, the Saracen raid of 846 having alarmed the city. He rebuilt Rome's walls, first enclosed the Vatican hill with the Leonine Wall, fortified Civitavecchia in 854 (renamed Leopoli), and organized a league of Italian cities that defeated the Saracen fleet at Ostia in 849. At a Roman synod in April 850 he crowned Louis II co-emperor.
b.s: The works held here are his letters and decrees on episcopal jurisdiction, ordination, excommunication, and warfare, together with a homily; they show a ninth-century pope legislating on the boundaries of dioceses and the accountability of pastors.

w: Acts of the Translation of St. Mennas
On the Dedication of the Church of Monte Cassino

b.bio: Leo Marsicanus, called Leo of Ostia from his later see, was born in Marsica around 1045/1046 and entered Monte Cassino at about fourteen. His talents won the regard of Abbot Desiderius, later Pope Victor III, who entrusted his education to the future Cardinal Aldemar. He became the abbey's librarian and archivist, settling property disputes from its documents. Abbot Oderisius set him to write a history of the monastery; from about 1099 to 1103 he composed the Chronica Monasterii Casinensis, covering 529 to 1075, drawing on Amatus's earlier work, oral tradition, and above all the abbey charters. Urban II made him cardinal deacon in 1088, and Paschal II promoted him cardinal bishop of Ostia in 1101; he defended the papacy against Henry V. He died on May 22, in 1115, 1116, or 1117.
b.s: His chronicle is the principal source for Monte Cassino's history to 1075 and a valuable mine of information for southern Italian affairs generally; Peter the Deacon continued it to 1139, and modern scholarship distinguishes Leo's own revised recension from later Cassinese reworkings — the very questions the texts here address.

b.bio: Leo was bishop of Sens in sixth-century Gaul, successor to Saint Paul in that see. He attended the councils of Orléans — the second through a vicar, the third in person — and entrusted the evangelization of Melun to Saint Aspose. He defended the rights of his see against King Childebert I and died in 541; he was buried at Sens in the church of Saints Gervais and Protais.
b.s: The library holds his letter to Childebert I, a polemical protest asserting that no second bishop may be ordained while the first lives, that petitioners for a new bishop are deserters, and that unauthorized ordainers incur excommunication until papal or synodal judgment.

b.bio: Leo VI was a Roman, son of the primicerius Christophorus, and cardinal-priest of Santa Susanna before his election as pope in mid-928, an election arranged by the senatrix Marozia after she had deposed John X. His pontificate lasted about seven months, during the Saeculum obscurum. Sources disagree on the exact dates: some give death on 12 February 929; Britannica says probably December 928. He confirmed the decisions of the Synod of Spalato and settled jurisdictional disputes in Dalmatia.
b.s: The single epistle held here is his bull regulating Dalmatian church order: it grants the pallium to Archbishop John of Spalato, confines bishops to their ancient diocesan limits, orders Bishop Gregory of the Croats to keep to Scodra, and threatens usurping bishops with excommunication.

b.bio: Leo VII was a Roman, priest of San Sisto and probably a Benedictine monk, elected pope on 3 January 936 under the control of Alberic II of Spoleto, who secured his election after the death of John XI. His three-year pontificate was spent largely issuing bulls of privilege to monasteries, especially Cluny; he summoned Odo of Cluny to negotiate peace between Alberic and Hugh, king of Italy, and named Frederick of Mainz his vicar for reform in Germany, forbidding forced baptism of Jews while permitting their expulsion if unbaptized.
b.s: The letters and privileges held here are chiefly monastic grants asserting exemption from all jurisdiction save the apostolic see, free abbatial election per Benedict's rule, and anathema against violators of papal privilege—documents that show how 10th-century papal authority operated through privilege rather than doctrine.

b.bio: Leo VIII was a Roman, son of John, who held the office of protonotary, and himself served as protoscriniarius in the papal court during the pontificate of John XII. In December 963 a synod convened by Emperor Otto I deposed John XII and elected Leo, then a layman; he received all orders at once and was consecrated on 6 December 963. Expelled when Otto left Rome in February 964, he fled to the emperor, returned after Benedict V's deposition, and reigned from 23 June 964 until his death on 1 March 965 (the Catholic Encyclopedia gives only 'between 20 February and 13 April 965'). He is today considered by the Catholic Church to have been an antipope during his first period and the legitimate pope during the second.
b.s: His pontificate is a test case of imperial control over papal elections after the saeculum obscurum; the privileges held here concern episcopal election, the pallium, and Aquileia's rank among Italian churches.

w: Letter to Kings Hugh and Robert

b.bio: Leo was a Benedictine abbot in Rome and a frequent papal legate after 992. He became the second abbot of Santi Bonifacio ed Alessio on the Aventine in 981, succeeding Sergius of Damascus; the house followed the Benedictine rule and also housed Basilian monks. Adalbert of Prague took refuge there as a monk during his exiles from his see (990–992 and 994–996), and Leo is praised in Adalbert's earliest biography (Vita prior) as 'simple, a friend of the Psalms and always ready to preach'. During the reign of Pope Benedict VII he examined the theology of James of Carthage for orthodoxy. He crossed the Alps three times on papal business as legate.
b.s: The library holds his letter to Kings Hugh and Robert, which treats the Church, true worship, and Scripture — evidence of a Roman abbot-legate addressing the West Frankish kings on ecclesiastical matters.

w: Prayer on Blessed Robert of Arbrissel

b.bio: The library prints this name as 'Leodegar of Bourges' and holds under it a single item in PL 162: a prayer on Blessed Robert of Arbrissel, founder of Fontevraud, who died in 1116. That work places its author in the early twelfth century and in the circle connected with Robert's cult. It does not match the better-attested Saint Leodegar (Léger), bishop of Autun, martyred c. 677–679, whose life and martyrdom are covered by the sources consulted here; that seventh-century bishop is a different person and is not the author of the work held.
b.s: The single work held is a devotional prayer on Robert of Arbrissel, evidence for the early cult of the Fontevraud founder among twelfth-century Latin writers.

b.bio: Leodegar (Leodegarius), son of the nobleman Bodilon (also given as Bobilo) and Sigrada, was raised at the court of Clotaire II, educated at Poitiers under his uncle the bishop, and became abbot of St. Maxentius, where he introduced the Rule of St. Benedict. Summoned by Queen Bathildis to assist in governing the kingdom, he was made Bishop of Autun and held a reforming council there in 661. He led the Burgundian faction against Ebroin, Mayor of the Palace of Neustria; accused of complicity in Childeric's murder, he was mutilated and executed at Sarcing in 678 or 679 (sources give both years), and venerated as a martyr.
b.s: The works held here are chiefly his Testament, a dying disposition of goods that transfers villas to the church of Autun, endows monks to pray perpetually for kingdom and princes, binds successor bishops to observe the donation, and anathematizes violators with Judas, Dathan, and Abiron.

b.bio: Leodegar of Vienne (Leodegarius Viennensis) was an eleventh-century archbishop of Vienne; Documenta Catholica Omnia dates his activity to 1037–1067 and lists his Chartae, a Council of Tours (AD 1060), and a life with works drawn from Gallia Christiana. He is not the seventh-century Saint Leodegar (Léger), bishop of Autun and martyr (d. 678), whom some encyclopedias describe under the same name; that man belongs to a different century entirely and is ignored here. The charters held in this library concern church property, episcopal authority, and a marchioness's pledge against coin falsification.
b.s: The single work held here is a set of charters asserting that the power of binding and loosing passed from Peter to bishops, that alienated church property must be restored, and that disturbers of ecclesiastical donations incur anathema.

w: On the Model of a Petition

b.bio: Leodevaldus was a Frank who died around 580; the Heiligenlexikon identifies him as bishop of Avranches and records that Robert of Langres and others called him a saint. The single page held here under his name, De exemplari praecariae, is a model document: a form for a precarial petition in which a petitioner holds church property in usufruct without right of alienation, owes an annual census in kind to the mother church, and whose monastery reverts to the bishop upon the holder's death.
b.s: The single page preserved under his name is a legal-ecclesiastical formulary showing how Merovingian bishops managed landed property held by petitioners on the church's terms.

b.bio: Leotaldus of Mâcon (Leotaldus Matisconensis) is known from a single document: a charter in which he, styled 'comes Matisconensis' by God's grace, together with his wife Ermengardis, grants property at Dardanicum in the pagus of Lyon on the Sillia river to the monastery of Cluny, then under Abbot Odo. The charter states the gift is made for love of God and eternal retribution, so that God may free their souls and those of their parents Albericus, Tholosana, Manasseus, Ermengardis, and their friend Geraldus from the punishments of hell. It closes with witnesses including Count Gaufredus and a penalty clause against violators.
b.s: His sole surviving work is the donation charter to Cluny printed in PL 133, cols. 841–844A, an early witness to Cluniac landholding and to the theology of almsgiving as liberation of souls from hell's punishment.

w: Book on the Attire of Clerics

b.bio: Leovigild was a priest of ninth-century Córdoba, a member of the Mozarabic Christian community living under Umayyad emir rule. Sources name him among the Cordoban clergy who sustained the church there against pressure from the emirs' court and Muslim proselytism, and he is counted with the Martyrs of Córdoba: Catholic Online records his death in 852 under Abd al-Rahman II. The Spanish source on De habitu clericorum says he probably studied under St. Eulogius and Abbot Speraindeo. He should not be confused with Leovigild, the sixth-century Arian Visigothic king.
b.s: The library holds his Book on the Attire of Clerics (De habitu clericorum), which argues that clerical dress bears mystical meaning and that clerics must not adopt the garb of the Ishmaelites — a document of Christian identity under Islamic rule in ninth-century Córdoba.

b.bio: A native of Gaul who embraced asceticism under Cassian at Marseilles about the opening of the fifth century, where he enjoyed a reputation for purity and holiness. He advanced the view that man did not need divine grace and that Christ was born with a human nature only, and was excommunicated for these doctrines. He went to Africa, became familiar with Aurelius and St. Augustine, became convinced of his errors, and drew up a solemn recantation addressed to Proculus, bishop of Marseilles, and Cyllinnius, bishop of Aix, with four African prelates bearing witness to his conversion. Laying aside the profession of a monk, he was ordained a presbyter by St. Augustine in A.D. 425, and appears to be the Leporius praised in the De Vita et Moribus Clericorum. Nothing further is known except that he was still alive in 430 (Cassianus, De Incarn. 1:4).
b.s: The Booklet of Emendation held here is that recantation: a public retraction of his former Christology, now confessing that God himself was born of the Virgin Mary, that the Word became flesh without conversion or mutability, that God mixes with flesh without diminution of substance, that flesh is assumed by the Word rather than the Word absorbed by flesh, and that the incarnation is a personal, not natural, union — arguing against his own former letter, error, and exegesis.

w: Book of Miracles of Saint Maximinus
Life of St. Julian of Le Mans
Translation of the Body of St. Junian

b.bio: Letaldus of Micy was a Benedictine monk of the abbey of Micy (Saint-Mesmin) on the Loire near Orléans, active in the later tenth century; Biblissima gives c. 945–996. He wrote Latin hagiography and miracle collections: a Liber miraculorum sancti Maximini, a Historia of St. Julian of Le Mans, and an account of the translation (Delatio) of St. Junian's body to the synod of Charroux. The works held here defend the claim that God, not man, works miracles through his saints, that nothing pleases God except what is true, and that pagans worship the creature rather than the Creator.
b.s: His hagiographic texts are evidence for tenth-century monastic teaching on relics, miracle, and true worship; the works held here include polemic against Claudius of Turin's position.

w: Summary of the Case of the Nestorians and Eutychians

b.bio: Liberatus was an archdeacon of the Church of Carthage. In 535 he went to Rome as legate of an African synod of 217 bishops to consult Pope Agapetus I. He opposed Justinian's edict against the Three Chapters (544) and served repeatedly as ambassador for the African bishops in that dispute. He followed Bishop Reparatus of Carthage to Constantinople in 551; after Reparatus's deposition and exile to Pontus (552), Liberatus was forced to join him there following the Council of Constantinople II (553). On Reparatus's death (563) he apparently returned to Africa. His stated aim in writing was to show how misjudged Justinian's condemnation of the Three Chapters was.
b.s: His Breviarium causae Nestorianorum et Eutychianorum is a principal narrative source for the Nestorian and Monophysite controversies from Nestorius's ordination (428) to the Fifth Ecumenical Council (553), written from a Chalcedonian, anti-Three-Chapters standpoint.

b.bio: Licinian was bishop of Cartagena (Carthago Spartaria) during the Byzantine occupation of southeastern Spain in the late sixth century. His correspondence with Pope Gregory the Great (590–601) and with Eutropius of Valencia places him in the second half of that century; Isidore of Seville records him as learned in the Scriptures and praises him in De viris illustribus. Only three of his letters survive: one to Gregory the Great, one to the deacon Epiphanius, and one to Vincent, bishop of Ibiza. Isidore reports that he was famous in the time of Mauricius Augustus, that he is buried in Constantinople, and that he was 'poisoned they say, murdered by a rival.' The Spanish Wikipedia account gives his death at Constantinople in 602 and argues that the common claim that Leovigild exiled him cannot be right, since Leovigild was dead and Cartagena lay under Byzantine sovereignty when Licinian left for Constantinople.
b.s: His three surviving letters are among the few witnesses to theological debate in Byzantine-ruled Spania, defending against opponents who denied that angels are spirits and engaging Augustine's and Origen's positions on the soul and creation.

w: Charter on the establishment of regular canons

b.bio: Lietbert of Cambrai, of Brabantian noble birth at Opbrakel, served as archdeacon and provost of the cathedral of Cambrai before his election as bishop on 31 March 1051; he held the see until his death on 28 September 1076. In 1054 he led a pilgrimage toward Jerusalem that reached only Cyprus before turning back. His biographer Raoul of Saint-Sépulcre also credits him with local reforms of religious houses in Flanders and western Francia. The sources give slightly different birth years (infobox c. 1000; article text ca. 1010); both are noted here.
b.s: The single work held here is a short charter establishing regular canons, arguing that common life without private property restores proper divine worship against secular canons who retain property.

b.bio: Lietbert was a regular canon of Saint-Ruf in the diocese of Avignon (from 1096), becoming its abbot around 1100; his successor is attested by 1111. Educated at the collegiate church of Saint-Pierre at Lille, he is also called Letbert of Lille. He wrote the Liber ecclesiastici et canonici ordinis, a customary for Saint-Ruf grounded in Augustine's monastic teaching and influential on later houses of Augustinian canons. A commentary on the Psalms, the Flores Psalmorum, is also attributed to him.
b.s: The letters held here defend the divine institution and dignity of the clerical order — priests as mediators with power to absolve sins, linen vestments as signs of chastity — themes consistent with his customary's program of canonical reform.

b.bio: Dom Jean Liron was a Benedictine monk of the Congregation of Saint-Maur, born at Chartres on 11 November 1665. Professed at about twenty, he worked in Paris with Dom Lenourry on the Apparatus ad Bibliothecam SS. Patrum (1703-1715), then arranged the archives of the abbey of Marmoutier near Tours, and ended his life at Le Mans. Sources disagree on his death date: CTHS gives 9 February 1749 at Le Mans, while another account gives 1 July 1748. He wrote polemical antiquarian works, including an Apologie pour les Armoricains (1708) against Dom Lobineau and a dissertation against Basnage on the Jews in France.
b.s: The two pieces held here are his dissertation and Life of St. Victor in PL 58, which sort out which Victor wrote the Vandal persecution history: the historian is Victor of Vita, not Victor bishop of Vite or of Utica; Victor became bishop only after Huneric's death and acted as cleric, not bishop, under the persecutions — correcting Rhenanus's attribution and Chifflet's biography.

b.bio: The name Lisiard of Tours is attached to the Secunda pars historiae Iherosolimitane, a narrative of the Latin settlement in Outremer after the First Crusade. Andrew D. Buck's study places that text in northeastern France in the early 1150s and connects it with the Premonstratensian order and a church council held at Laon Cathedral in March 1150. The attribution to Lisiard is traditional ('often attributed'), and no source here gives dates or offices for him. Migne printed his surviving scripta in PL 1854 alongside works of Godefrid of Admont and Hariulf.
b.s: His History of Jerusalem, held here, narrates the early Latin kingdom — Godfrey's refusal of the crown, Baldwin's lawful coronation, wars against Saracens and Turks — reading events through providence and divine judgment on sin.

b.bio: The library prints this author as 'Livinus of Metz,' but the work it holds decides who he is: the single-page epistle in PL 87 cites 'Father Florbert,' which identifies him as Livinus of Ghent. Livinus was said to be of Irish birth, a bishop, and a preacher in Flanders and Zeeland, martyred at Esse near Geraardsbergen; his historicity has been questioned because his Passio borrows from the life of Lebuinus of Deventer.
b.s: The epistle here, addressed to Florbert of Ghent, is one of only two texts on which any claim to Livinus's existence rests (the other being an epitaph on St Bavo), and its genuineness was first challenged by Rettberg.

b.bio: Lonegisilus calls himself an unworthy priest and a monk by will though not by habit. In his charter he recounts leaving his noble, wealthy Alamannian parents, who pressed him toward pagan worship and royal military service; instructed and baptized by Christians he met, he wandered to the pays Cenomanais and built a small monastery at the vicus Busiacus. In 625 he donated it, with all he had acquired or could acquire, to Hadoindus, bishop of Le Mans, and his church, under King Clothar II. A later lexicon lists him as a saint, a priest of Mans.
b.s: The single work held here is his foundation charter of 625, valuable for monastic donation practice, episcopal control of new monasteries, and a convert's own account of leaving paganism.

w: Sermon on the Elevation of the Body of St. Amandus

b.bio: Lotharius I Germaniae is Lothair I, eldest son of Emperor Louis the Pious and grandson of Charlemagne, born in 795. He was made king of Bavaria after Louis's accession in 814, joint emperor by the Ordinatio imperii of 817, and king of Italy from 818. He repeatedly rebelled against his father over the claims of Charles the Bald, fought his brothers Louis the German and Charles in the war of 840–843, and received Middle Francia at the Treaty of Verdun. He died on 29 September 855 at the Abbey of Prüm. The works held here are capitularies, letters (including one to Rabanus Maurus), and a sermon.
b.s: The library holds his capitularies and letters — documents of imperial church governance from a Carolingian emperor whose reign shaped the division of Charlemagne's empire.

w: Sacrament concerning the reception of Theutberga

b.bio: Lothar II, second son of Emperor Lothar I, ruled Lotharingia from 855 until his death at Piacenza in August 869. Sources give his birth variously as 827, c. 835, or c. 837; his death is dated 7 or 8 August 869. He is known chiefly for his decade-long attempt to dissolve his marriage to Teutberga so as to remarry Waldrada, which brought him into conflict with Pope Nicholas I and his uncles Charles the Bald and Louis the German.
b.s: The work held here is his Sacramentum de Theotberga recipienda, the oath by which he undertook to take back his lawful wife Teutberga — a document from the divorce case that made royal marriage discipline a matter of papal authority.

b.bio: Lothair of Supplinburg, son of the Saxon count Gebhard of Supplinburg, was appointed Duke of Saxony in 1106 and elected King of Germany in 1125 before being crowned emperor in Rome on 4 June 1133. His reign was troubled by Hohenstaufen opposition under Duke Frederick II of Swabia and Duke Conrad of Franconia. He died on 4 December 1137 at Breitenwang while returning from a campaign against the Norman Kingdom of Sicily.
b.s: The two documents held here are his coronation rite of 4 June 1133 ('Coronatio') and a sentence against Pope Anacletus dated 3 June 1133 ('In Anacletum Papam Sententia'). The texts present the king/emperor as divinely appointed defender of the Roman church, swearing protection of the pope's person and restoration of Peter's regalia to the church, and condemning Peter Leonis (Anacletus) and his accomplices as schismatics who break faith — primary evidence for imperial-papal relations at the end of the investiture controversy.

b.bio: Jean de Launoy (Joannes Launoius), born at Le Valdécie near Valognes in Normandy, studied philosophy and theology at the College of Navarre in Paris, received his licenciate and doctorate in 1634, was ordained priest in 1636, and spent his life as a critical historian attached to the Sorbonne, never seeking ecclesiastical promotion. He was a Gallican in church politics and Jansenist-leaning in theology, a rigorous critic of hagiography and false attributions (known as 'le dénicheur des saints'), who preferred expulsion from the Sorbonne to endorsing the condemnation of Arnauld.
b.s: The two sets of notes held here are his historical-critical dissertations on Hildebert of Le Mans, using Ivo of Chartres, the Chronicle of Tours, Ordericus Vitalis, and Suger to defend Hildebert against charges fabricated by envious clerics of Le Mans, against William's acquisition of Le Mans by deceit, and against Malmesbury and Juretus.

b.bio: Lucas of Tuy (O Tudense) was a Leonese cleric, canon of San Isidoro in León from 1221 to 1239, then Bishop of Tuy until his death in 1249 (one older source gives 1250). He traveled widely—to Rome, Constantinople, Jerusalem, Armenia, and France—and wrote at the request of Queen Berenguela of León-Castile. His major work is the Chronicon mundi (completed 1236), a four-part world chronicle drawing chiefly on Isidore of Seville; he also wrote against Cathar errors and on the miracles of St. Isidore.
b.s: The library holds his Life of St. Martin, a hagiographical-exegetical piece asserting that saints' merits and prayers avail with God, that pilgrimage and vows merit grace, and that scriptural understanding comes by divine illumination—against Jews and heretics.

b.bio: A presbyter of Caphamargala (Caphargamala), writing in Latin in the fifth century. The Documenta Catholica Omnia index dates him 354–430; Wikidata and the Vatican Library authority file place him only in the fifth century, so the narrower range is given here. He is not to be confused with Lucian of Antioch, the earlier martyr-theologian. The one work held under his name is a letter to the whole Church recounting how the relics of Stephen the protomartyr were found.
b.s: His Epistola ad omnem Ecclesiam is a principal Latin account of the discovery of St Stephen's relics, narrating Gamaliel's revelatory appearances and asserting that God revealed the relics' location by vision, that relics of saints must be revealed and honored, that God preserves the bodies of his martyrs, and that sharing with martyrs secures a share in resurrection.

w: On Not Sparing Those Who Sin Against God
That one must die for the Son of God

b.bio: Bishop of Cagliari in Sardinia, first appearing in the record in 354 as an envoy sent by Pope Liberius to Emperor Constantius II to request a council on Athanasius's case. At Milan (355) he defended Athanasius against Arian condemnation; with Eusebius of Vercelli he was exiled by Constantius, first to Germanicia in Syria, then Palestine, finally the Thebaid. He wrote his polemical pamphlets during exile and returned after Constantius's death. Sources give his death as 370 (Wikipedia, DLL) or 371 (Catholic Encyclopedia); Britannica says c. 370.
b.s: The works held here are his anti-Arian polemics from exile: letters on excommunication and separation from heretics, defenses of Athanasius, and tracts arguing that kings who persecute the church answer to priestly rebuke and divine punishment.

b.bio:
Lucifer of Cagliari (d. 370 or 371) — Bishop of Cagliari in Sardinia, first appearing in the record in 354 as an envoy sent by Pope Liberius to Emperor Constantius II to request a council on Athanasius's case. At Milan (355) he defended Athanasius against Arian condemnation; with Eusebius of Vercelli he was exiled by Constantius, first to Germanicia in Syria, then Palestine, finally the Thebaid. He wrote his polemical pamphlets during exile and returned after Constantius's death. Sources give his death as 370 (Wikipedia, DLL) or 371 (Catholic Encyclopedia); Britannica says c. 370.

Hilary (c. c. 310–c. 367) — Hilary was born at Poitiers at the beginning of the fourth century to a noble, very probably pagan family. Having taken up the study of Holy Scripture, he found there the truth he sought, renounced idolatry, and was baptized. His learning and zeal led to his being chosen about 350 to govern the church of Poitiers. He championed orthodoxy against Arianism, which threatened Gaul, and was the first Latin writer to introduce Greek doctrine to Western Christendom.

Pancratius the presbyter (fl. 355) — The Pancratius who wrote this letter is not the boy martyr Pancras of the Via Aurelia (d. c. 304), despite the shared name; the dictionary sources describe the martyr, a different person, and are not used for this author. This Pancratius was a presbyter of Rome banished from Milan in 355, apparently alongside other bishops and clergy exiled there under imperial pressure (the circle including Hilary of Poitiers and Lucifer of Cagliari, with whom he is associated in the sources). He is attested by Hilary of Poitiers' historical fragments, Lucifer of Cagliari, Athanasius' Historia Arianorum, Jerome, and Prosper of Aquitaine. He could have been recalled along with the others banished in Milan in 355, in 362 or earlier, but his fate afterwards is unknown.
b.s: The works held here are his anti-Arian polemics from exile: letters on excommunication and separation from heretics, defenses of Athanasius, and tracts arguing that kings who persecute the church answer to priestly rebuke and divine punishment.

b.bio: Gherardo Caccianemici dal Orso, born in Bologna, was for many years a canon of the Basilica di San Frediano before being made a cardinal by Pope Callixtus II (1123). Innocent II appointed him papal chancellor, in which role he aided the pope against the antipope Anacletus II. Elected pope in March 1144 to succeed Celestine II, he faced the invasion of papal lands by Roger II of Sicily and the Roman Commune under Giordano Pierleoni, which proclaimed a republic free from papal civil rule. He led an unsuccessful assault against the rebels and died on 15 February 1145, presumably from injuries suffered in the fighting.
b.s: The letters and privileges held here are papal instruments defending monastery possessions, exemptions (such as monks' tithe exemption on their own labor), and papal privilege under threat of excommunication, directed against diocesan bishops and local magnates like Godefridus of Dol and the count of Nevers.

b.bio:
Ludovicus I Franciae (778–840) — Ludovicus I Franciae is Louis the Pious (Hludowicus Pius), son of Charlemagne and Hildegard and the only surviving son of that marriage. He was born at Casseneuil in 778, was King of Aquitaine from 781, co-emperor with his father from 813, and sole ruler of the Franks from 814 until his death on 20 June 840, apart from his deposition from November 833 to March 834 amid the civil wars with his sons Lothair, Pepin, and Louis. The works held here are capitularies — imperial legislative texts regulating church order, worship, sacraments, and clerical conduct — which explains their placement among Latin ecclesiastical authors. A separate source describing a Sancti Ludovici Francorum regis (vita printed 1617, with Boniface VIII's canonization sermons and bull) concerns Louis IX, canonized in 1297; that is a different person and not this author.

Lotharius I Germaniae (795–855) — Lotharius I Germaniae is Lothair I, eldest son of Emperor Louis the Pious and grandson of Charlemagne, born in 795. He was made king of Bavaria after Louis's accession in 814, joint emperor by the Ordinatio imperii of 817, and king of Italy from 818. He repeatedly rebelled against his father over the claims of Charles the Bald, fought his brothers Louis the German and Charles in the war of 840–843, and received Middle Francia at the Treaty of Verdun. He died on 29 September 855 at the Abbey of Prüm. The works held here are capitularies, letters (including one to Rabanus Maurus), and a sermon.
b.s: The capitularies held here show an emperor legislating directly for the church — its worship, sacraments, discipline, and property — making them primary evidence for Carolingian church-state relations.

w: Constitution on raising the army of Benevento

b.bio: Ludovicus II Germaniae is Louis the German, grandson of Charlemagne and third son of Louis the Pious, who received the East Frankish kingdom by the Treaty of Verdun in 843 and ruled until his death at Frankfurt in 876. The works held here are his capitularies and diplomas — royal chapters on church discipline, oaths, marriage within forbidden degrees, clerical conduct, and the emperor's duty to enforce correction when admonition fails. Note: the Wikisource headers for these texts label them 'saeculo X', while the biographical sources identify the author as the ninth-century king.
b.s: His capitularies show a Carolingian king legislating directly on ecclesiastical morals, sacramental discipline, and the relation of royal to episcopal authority.

b.bio: Louis II, called the Younger, son of Lothair I, was crowned king of Italy in 844 and co-emperor with his father until 855, ruling alone thereafter. He took Bari from the Aghlabids in 871 and thereafter styled himself imperator Romanorum, a title that strained relations with Byzantium. The library holds a single chapter under his name (PL 138), a historical text asserting that property assigned to evade justice falls under ban. His charters issued at Pavia confirm privileges to monasteries and patriarchates, including the 855 confirmation of Lothair's charter to the Patriarchate of Aquileia granting metropolitan jurisdiction over the Istrian bishoprics, a dispute settled at the Synod of Mantua (827).
b.s: The work held here is a one-page historical chapter on property assigned to evade justice falling under ban; Louis matters chiefly as the Carolingian emperor whose diplomas shaped Italian ecclesiastical jurisdiction.

b.bio:
Ludovicus IV Franciae (c. 920–954) — Louis IV, called d'Outremer because he was raised in England at the court of Wessex, was the son of Charles the Simple and Eadgifu of Wessex. Recalled from exile after Rudolph's death, he was crowned at Laon in 936 and reigned over West Francia until his death in 954. His reign is known chiefly through Flodoard's annals and Richer's history. The work held here is not theology but a royal diploma of 939: a precept confirming Cluny's exemption from all human dominion, its right to elect its own abbot by rule, and the immunity of church property and tithes from seizure.

Conradus imperator (unknown) — The name as printed points to an emperor named Conrad, but no source in hand describes this figure: The surviving records cover Conrad Celtes the Renaissance humanist, Conrad of Saxony the Franciscan, and Conradus Teutonicus the penitential writer — all different men, all disregarded here. No source gives dates or biography for the emperor. The single work held here fits an imperial-style diploma concerning Cluny, asserting papal protection without lordship over the abbey, free abbatial election by the monks, immunity of church property and tithes from seizure, and the irrevocability of donations made to God.
b.s: His 939 precept for Cluny is an early royal charter of monastic liberty, asserting that kings must subject their power to God's will, that donations to God are irrevocable despite monastic fault, that kings are bound to exalt and assist the church, and that no pact may subject Cluny to any mortal — including the principle of papal protection without lordship over monasteries.

w: Diploma granted to Hetto of Basel

b.bio: Louis the Pious, son and successor of Charlemagne, ruled as king of the Franks and Holy Roman Emperor from 814 until his death in 840. His reign is documented by contemporary biographies: Thegan of Trier's Gesta Hludowici Imperatoris (836–7) and the anonymous Vita Hludovici written in Latin in or soon after 840 by an author conventionally called the Astronomer, who held office at Louis's court. The works held under his name are not treatises but acts of government: diplomas, letters, privileges, and charters in which he grants churches and monasteries immunity from secular jurisdiction, confirms monks' right to elect their abbots, and frames gifts and alms to holy places as earning heavenly reward.
b.s: The documents here show how a Carolingian ruler used imperial diplomas to define the legal standing of the Church — immunity from judges, monastic self-election, and protection of worship — making them primary evidence for early medieval church-state relations.

w: Letter on His Capture and Liberation
Privileges granted to St. Denis in the time of Abbot Suger

b.bio: Louis VII, called the Younger, was king of France from 1137 until his death in 1180. Second son of Louis VI, he was first prepared for a career in the Church and became heir after his brother Philip's death in 1131. He married Eleanor of Aquitaine in 1137 and led the French contingent on the Second Crusade (1147–1149), which ended in failure before Damascus. With his counsellor Abbot Suger he pursued centralisation of royal government and patronised Gothic building, including Notre-Dame de Paris. His reign saw the founding of the University of Paris.
b.s: The works held here are letters and documents issuing from his kingship: an account of his capture and liberation on the Second Crusade framing defeat as divine punishment for sin and slain crusaders as martyrs, and privileges granted to Saint-Denis under Abbot Suger.

b.bio: Liutbert (also printed Ludbert) was Archbishop of Mainz from 863 until his death in 889. He became Abbot of Ellwangen in 874 and is reckoned the first Archchancellor of Germany. He was archchaplain to Louis the German from 870 until 876 and then to Louis the Younger until 882, though he lost that court office under Charles the Fat. He presided over the synod of Worms in May 868, which condemned the Greek church for heresy, and helped organize the defence of East Francia against Viking attack. The Annales Fuldenses were written in his circle after 882.
b.s: The letter held here, addressed to King Louis, defends the primacy of the see of Peter and argues that a silent bishop is a hireling rather than a shepherd, that corruption at the head spreads to the body's members, and that unity among churches can be restored by cutting off incurable members and removing scandals.

b.bio: The name is a seventeenth-century invention attached to the Annales Lupi Protospatharii (Chronicon rerum in regno Neapolitano gestarum), a concise Latin chronicle of southern Italy covering 805 to 1102 (with surviving annalistic entries from 855). Nothing is known of the compiler beyond what the text shows: he wrote at Bari, drew on lost Bariot and Matera annals, and dated years from September. A Brindisi column naming a ninth-century Lupus Protospatharius does not identify him.
b.s: The chronicle held here is a primary source for Norman conquest-era Apulia — useful chronological information for Robert Guiscard's career and post-1085 Apulia, and material on Byzantine-Norman warfare — read through a providential lens that blames defeats on the people's sins.

b.bio: Lupus (French: Loup) was born at Toul in north-eastern Gaul to a noble family, worked as a lawyer, and married Pimeniola, sister of Hilary of Arles. After about six or seven years the couple separated by mutual vow of continency; Lupus sold his estates, gave the proceeds to the poor, and spent roughly a year as a monk at Lérins under Honoratus. Chosen bishop of Troyes around 426–427, he joined Germanus of Auxerre on the mission to Britain against Pelagianism. A sixth-century Life presents him as an ideal bishop and healer; it also reports that his prayers spared Troyes from Attila's Huns.
b.s: The letters held here treat episcopal office as humble service — pastors sustain a suffering church, ministers must be servants of all, and worldly gifts belong to divine use — themes consistent with the ideal-bishop portrait of his hagiography.

w: Ceremonies observed in the cathedral church of Rouen

b.bio: The name 'L. Patry' as printed in the library record does not correspond to any identifiable author in the surviving records, which describe modern academics of the same or similar names and are disregarded here. The work held under this name is a one-page historical account of ceremonies at the cathedral church of Rouen, printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 147 among medieval Norman liturgical materials. Nothing about the compiler's dates, office, or life is established by the sources given.
b.s: The piece records how honor to prelates was distinguished from adoration of the sacrament, detailing gestures such as the epistle reader's simple reverence without hand-kissing, the assistant priest kissing the prelate's hand at incensing, and the prelate granting pontifical blessing at mass and vespers.

b.bio: Laurentius Surius was born in Lübeck (sources give 1522 or 1523) to a goldsmith's family and studied at Frankfort-on-the-Oder and Cologne, taking a master's degree at Cologne in 1539. Peter Canisius, a fellow student at Cologne, apparently received him into the Church from a Protestant background. In 1542 Lanspergius drew him into the Carthusian monastery of Saint Barbara in Cologne, where he spent nearly his whole life as priest and scholar, translating ascetical writers (Tauler, Suso/Seuse, Ruysbroeck) into Latin and writing on hagiography and church history. He died at Cologne in May 1578 (the Catholic Encyclopedia gives 23 May; Wikipedia gives 25 May). Note: the single item shelved here under his name, an 'Admonition' in PL 98, belongs to a medieval volume of the Patrologia Latina and cannot be the work of this sixteenth-century author; it is presumably a different writer or a misattributed text.
b.s: A Counter-Reformation hagiographer and translator whose editions shaped Catholic reading of the saints; the 'Admonition' held here under his name sits in a medieval Patrologia Latina volume and does not match his dates.

b.bio: Louis Thomassin, born at Aix-en-Provence on 28 August 1619 and died in Paris on 24 December 1695, entered the Oratory at thirteen, taught literature in its colleges and theology at Saumur, then lectured in positive theology at the seminary of Saint-Magloire until his death. With Denis Pétau he was counted among the masters of positive theology; his major works include the Vetus et nova ecclesiae disciplina circa beneficia, the Dogmata theologica on the Incarnation and God's properties, and the Dissertationes in concilia generalia et particularia (1667). The library holds one short dissertation from him: a citation-survey defending the Roman practice of receiving heretical baptism without repetition.
b.s: The work held here argues that baptism with the trinitarian form is validated by the words themselves rather than the minister's faith, need not be repeated even when conferred by heretics, and that Cyprian and Firmilian were wrong to demand rebaptism—Cyprian excused only because no plenary council had yet decided.

b.bio: Luke Wadding (Lucas Waddingus), born at Waterford, Ireland, 16 October 1588, died at St. Isidore's College, Rome, 18 November 1657, was an Irish Franciscan friar, theologian, and historian. Educated in Portugal (Lisbon and Coimbra) and ordained in 1613, he spent most of his career in Rome, where he co-founded the Irish College and was associated with St. Isidore's. He is best known for his editions of Duns Scotus and his Annales Minorum, the history of the Franciscan order. The two pieces held under his name here are editorial matter: a forewarning defending the authenticity of works attributed to Anselm against objections from stylistic variety, and a short letter to Bivarius printed in a volume of Augustine's correspondence.
b.s: The works held here show him as an editor and defender of patristic and medieval attributions, arguing that varied style across an author's writings reflects varied subjects and audiences rather than spurious authorship.

b.bio: the surviving records describe two different men named Canossa: Baldassare Castiglione (1478–1529), the Renaissance courtier and author of The Book of the Courtier, and Luigi di Canossa (1809–1900), the Jesuit cardinal-bishop of Verona. Neither matches the author of the synodal constitutions printed in PL 147, which legislate on clerical dress, residence at benefices, concubinage, taverns in presbyteries, and reserved cases for absolution, citing Jerome's letter to Rusticus and 'the lord bishop of Bayeux' — a citation suggesting a Norman episcopal milieu (possibly eleventh-century, though the date is not established by any source here). No source gives dates, see, or biography for this Ludovico; he must be treated as otherwise unidentified.
b.s: His single held work is a short set of synodal constitutions enforcing clerical discipline — habit, residence, celibacy, and jurisdictional competence in absolution — apparently within an early Norman reform context (inferred from the citation of the bishop of Bayeux).
